news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 18, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Pediatric Bronchiolitis Study Analyzes Respiratory Pathogens and Hospital Recovery Times by November 12, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Pediatric Bronchiolitis Study Analyzes Respiratory Pathogens and Hospital Recovery Times Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A retrospective investigation conducted at Hebei Children’s Hospital in northern China has characterized the viral landscape of acute infant bronchiolitis, demonstrating that while respiratory syncytial virus and human rhinovirus represent the predominant infectious drivers, neither specific viral profiles nor polymicrobial infections significantly prolonged hospital recovery times. The clinical study, carried out in a tertiary-grade pediatric center located in Shijiazhuang, examined medical records spanning from September 2022 through February 2025 to determine how diverse viral agents influence hospitalization courses. Bronchiolitis remains the leading cause of acute lower respiratory tract infections requiring admission among children younger than two years of age, particularly presenting during the first six months of life with sudden-onset wheezing, cough, chest retractions, and auscultatory fine crackles. By evaluating clinical data from 132 hospitalized infants alongside advanced multiplex molecular diagnostic assays, the researchers sought to elucidate the local epidemiological patterns within a temperate, centrally heated continental climate and evaluate whether specific viral signatures altered hospital length of stay. Patient inclusion required children aged two years or younger who exhibited definitive clinical signs of acute bronchiolitis consistent with the 2024 edition of the Expert Consensus on the Diagnosis, Treatment, and Prevention of Bronchiolitis in Children, supported by respiratory specimen collection within twenty-four hours of admission. To isolate standard disease trajectories and minimize clinical confounding, investigators systematically excluded children diagnosed with congenital heart disease, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, underlying immunodeficiencies, or other severe systemic disorders, as well as individuals who received systemic corticosteroids or immunoglobulin therapy within one week prior to admission. The study cohort comprised 132 pediatric cases with an overall male-to-female ratio of 2.3 to 1, representing 92 boys and 40 girls. Across the entire cohort, the median age was 6.6 months, with infants under six months constituting 46.2 percent, children aged six to twelve months representing 37.9 percent, and toddlers between twelve and twenty-four months accounting for 15.9 percent. The overall median hospital length of stay was 6.0 days. Diagnostic assessment relied on multiplex reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction assays paired with capillary electrophoresis fragment analysis, utilizing the GenomeLab GeXP Genetic Analysis System from Beckman Coulter. Specimen collection was conducted within twenty-four hours of hospital admission by dedicated clinical nursing personnel, who gathered posterior nasopharyngeal secretions using sterile synthetic-fiber swabs or deep lower respiratory tract secretions through negative-pressure suction into viral preservation solution. A commercial thirteen-pathogen panel developed by Ningbo Health Gene Technologies was utilized to simultaneously detect influenza A virus, influenza A 09H1, seasonal influenza A H3N2, influenza B, human adenovirus, human bocavirus, human rhinovirus, human parainfluenza virus, Chlamydia, human metapneumovirus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, human coronavirus, and respiratory syncytial virus. Quality assurance protocols integrated human housekeeping genes as internal amplification controls alongside positive reference standards and negative controls to ensure specimen adequacy and rule out reaction inhibition. The authors noted that identifying pathogen nucleic acids confirms the presence of genetic material but cannot definitively distinguish active causative illness from asymptomatic carriage or prolonged viral shedding. Although the initial study protocol intended routine testing across all admissions, twenty of the 132 eligible patients did not undergo molecular diagnostic testing due to attending clinician discretion and variable resource availability. To prevent selection bias from skewing association analyses, investigators restricted all pathogen-outcome evaluations to the 112 tested patients while preserving the full 132-patient cohort for demographic descriptions. A dedicated sensitivity analysis was executed to determine whether systematic clinical divergences existed between the twenty untested children and the 112 tested counterparts. This comparative evaluation revealed no statistically significant differences regarding sex distribution, where males comprised 70.5 percent of the tested cohort versus 65.0 percent of the untested group, or the proportion of infants under six months of age, which was 48.2 percent versus 35.0 percent. Similarly, median age was 6.5 months among tested children compared to 8.8 months in the untested group, median hospital stay was 6.0 days versus 6.5 days, and rapid recovery rates were 46.4 percent versus 30.0 percent, indicating that restricting subsequent pathogen-recovery analyses carried minimal risk of distortion. Among the 112 children who completed molecular screening, the overall pathogen detection rate reached 88.4 percent, with 99 individuals testing positive for at least one respiratory organism. Single-pathogen infections were identified in 77 cases, accounting for 68.8 percent of tested children, whereas multi-pathogen mixed infections occurred in 22 patients, representing 19.6 percent of the tested cohort; thirteen children, or 11.6 percent, yielded negative results across the thirteen targeted pathogens. Respiratory syncytial virus emerged as the primary infectious agent, documented in 54.5 percent of tested cases, including 42 single infections and 19 mixed infections. Human rhinovirus represented the second most prevalent pathogen, detected in 31.3 percent of tested cases, comprising 19 single infections and 16 mixed presentations. Parainfluenza virus was identified in 6.3 percent of patients, presenting exclusively as isolated single infections. Human metapneumovirus was detected in 5.4 percent, influenza in 4.5 percent, Mycoplasma pneumoniae in 2.7 percent, human adenovirus in 1.8 percent, and human bocavirus in 0.9 percent. The combination of respiratory syncytial virus and human rhinovirus formed the most frequent mixed infection pattern, identified in eleven patients. Stratified evaluations revealed distinct age-related susceptibility patterns across the tested infant cohort. The detection frequencies for respiratory syncytial virus, human rhinovirus, and parainfluenza virus varied significantly across predefined age tiers of under six months, six to twelve months, and twelve to twenty-four months. Respiratory syncytial virus demonstrated elevated detection in younger cohorts, registering at 49 percent among infants younger than six months and 50 percent in those aged six to twelve months, before dropping significantly to 28 percent among toddlers aged twelve to twenty-four months. Human rhinovirus exhibited an even steeper age gradient favoring the youngest patients, appearing in 48 percent of infants under six months of age, but falling to 23 percent in the six-to-twelve-month group and 24 percent in the twelve-to-twenty-four-month bracket. Conversely, parainfluenza virus displayed an opposing trend, remaining rare among younger infants with a 1 percent detection rate in both the under-six-month and six-to-twelve-month groups, but increasing significantly to 10 percent among children aged twelve to twenty-four months. Pathogen activity demonstrated substantial seasonal variation within Shijiazhuang, characterized by a continental monsoon climate with cold, dry winters and prolonged centralized municipal heating running from mid-November to mid-March. This climate regime creates large indoor-outdoor temperature differentials and low indoor humidity, conditions known to enhance enveloped viral stability while drying mucosal barriers and impairing ciliary motility. Respiratory syncytial virus dominated the winter and early spring heating periods, reaching a monthly peak detection rate of 88.9 percent in February. Conversely, general hospital admissions declined during the summer and autumn months from June to October, but the relative positivity of alternative pathogens increased, with human rhinovirus reaching a peak proportion of 75.0 percent in June and parainfluenza virus reaching 66.7 percent in July. Intriguingly, an off-season epidemic surge of respiratory syncytial virus emerged in May, where overall pathogen testing yielded an 82.1 percent detection rate representing 23 positive cases among 28 tested patients. To evaluate whether this May epidemic represented a consistent annual pattern, researchers performed a descriptive sensitivity analysis tracking heating years from September to August. The data demonstrated that the May surge occurred almost exclusively during the 2022 to 2023 heating year, which recorded 27 tested patients in May with 23 testing positive for respiratory syncytial virus, alongside a diminished winter rate of 8.3 percent between December and March. In contrast, the subsequent 2023 to 2024 heating year recorded only a single tested patient in May, who tested negative, while exhibiting a pronounced winter wave from December to March where 22 of 27 tested children, or 81.5 percent, were positive for respiratory syncytial virus. The authors emphasized that because testing was not conducted as a continuous census and monthly enrollment numbers varied, these figures serve as descriptive sensitivity observations rather than evidence of a confirmed annual epidemiological shift. This temporal variation coincided with national adjustments in pandemic mitigation measures, leaving open whether the May surge represented an enduring regional phenomenon or a isolated post-restriction rebound. To assess clinical recovery speed, the investigators categorized patients using hospital length of stay, establishing a pragmatic threshold of five days or fewer for rapid recovery and greater than five days for delayed recovery. Within the 112 pathogen-tested patients, 52 children met criteria for rapid recovery while 60 experienced delayed recovery. Statistical comparison demonstrated no significant divergence between the groups regarding dominant viral pathogens or polymicrobial status. Respiratory syncytial virus was detected in 50.0 percent of rapid-recovery patients and 58.3 percent of delayed-recovery cases, human rhinovirus was present in 30.8 percent versus 31.7 percent, and mixed viral infections accounted for 13.5 percent versus 25.0 percent, respectively. While Mycoplasma pneumoniae and human bocavirus were detected exclusively in delayed-recovery cases, their low absolute frequencies precluded definitive association. Furthermore, while infants under six months represented 55.8 percent of the rapid-recovery group compared to 41.7 percent of the delayed-recovery cohort, this trend did not achieve statistical significance, illustrating that single or dual viral detections did not reliably predict prolonged clinical recovery. The authors emphasized that length of stay serves as a pragmatic operational metric influenced by complex non-biological factors, including parental anxiety, family economic circumstances, insurance mechanisms, clinician experience, and defensive medical practices aimed at preventing premature discharge or nosocomial exposure in vulnerable infants. Consequently, the lack of a statistically significant correlation between specific pathogens and recovery duration must be interpreted cautiously, as the single-center sample size limited statistical power for detecting subtle differences or analyzing low-frequency pathogens. Additional study limitations included the retrospective architecture, which precluded gathering standardized data on feeding practices, atopic predispositions, and secondhand tobacco smoke exposure, as well as the inherent diagnostic ambiguity between acute viral etiology and benign shedding. Nevertheless, because the overwhelming majority of documented bronchiolitis episodes were virally driven without clear evidence that multi-pathogen detection worsens recovery timelines, the researchers concluded that clinicians should strictly adhere to established antimicrobial stewardship principles, reserving empirical antibiotics and leveraging molecular testing to guide tailored supportive care. analysis.brief_en: A study conducted at Hebei Children’s Hospital in Shijiazhuang, northern China, analyzed the viral causes of acute infant bronchiolitis among 132 hospitalized infants aged two years or younger. The research, published on November 12, 2026, found that respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and human rhinovirus were the most common pathogens, accounting for 54.5% and a significant portion of cases, respectively. However, no statistically significant link was found between specific viral profiles or mixed infections and prolonged hospital recovery times. The study used advanced molecular diagnostic methods, including multiplex reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction assays, to detect pathogens. Despite a high detection rate of 88.4% among 112 tested patients, the authors noted that the single-center sample size may limit the ability to detect subtle differences in recovery duration. The research highlights the need for further studies to understand the impact of various pathogens on hospitalization outcomes in young children.

analysis_zh.location_and_population: 这项研究是在中国北方石家庄的河北省儿童医院进行的。涉及132名两岁及以下住院婴儿,男女比例为2.3比1。
analysis_zh.event: 一项回顾性研究分析了急性婴儿 毛细支气管炎 的病毒状况,确定 呼吸道合胞病毒 (RSV) 和人鼻病毒为主要病原体。研究发现,特定病毒特征或多微生物感染与医院康复时间延长之间没有显着相关性。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: Among 112 tested patients, RSV was the primary infectious agent, detected in 54.5 percent of cases. The overall pathogen detection rate was 88.4 percent, with 99 individuals testing positive for at least one respiratory organism. The median hospital length of stay was 6.0 days, with no significant differences in recovery duration linked to specific pathogens.
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 该研究使用多重分子诊断分析和毛细管电泳片段分析来检测病原体。由于临床医生的判断力和资源限制,它排除了 20 名未接受检测的患者。作者警告说,单中心样本量可能会限制检测细微差异的统计能力。

news.content_title: Flu, COVID-19 And RSV: What Marylanders Need To Know Before Thanksgiving
news.content: Health & Fitness Flu, COVID-19 And RSV: What Marylanders Need To Know Before Thanksgiving Thanksgiving brings families together just as the flu and respiratory virus season gets underway. Here's what you need to know. Influenza-related hospitalizations and deaths are already being reported in Maryland as families prepare to gather for Thanksgiving, starting a season of togetherness that gives respiratory viruses plenty of opportunities to spread. Nationally, seasonal flu activity is increasing in many areas, while viruses that commonly cause colds are circulating at elevated levels, according to the latest update from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. COVID-19 activity is declining nationally, with emergency department visits low and decreasing. Still, wastewater monitoring shows moderate levels of the virus circulating nationwide, with some states reporting high levels. Find out what's happening in Across Marylandfor free with the latest updates from Patch. RSV, or respiratory syncytial virus, usually causes cold-like symptoms but can be serious for infants and older adults. Emergency department visits remain low nationally but are increasing in many areas. Wastewater readings for RSV and influenza A remain very low nationally. In Maryland, CDC data suggests the respiratory illness level remains low, as do cases in neighboring Virginia. In D.C., officials say the level is "very low." Find out what's happening in Across Marylandfor free with the latest updates from Patch. However, the Maryland Department of Health's dashboard indicates wastewater monitoring showed high levels of COVID-19 activity. As of Oct. 4, MDH reported a total of 150 COVID-19-related hospitalizations. Eight deaths were recorded in October. When it comes to the seasonal flu, MDH's dashboard notes minimal activity, with influenza-like illnesses accounting for less than 3% of emergency room visits during the last week of October. Since Oct. 4, a total of 254 flu-related hospitalizations were recorded, along with two deaths. From late August to the start of November, RSV-related hospitalizations in Maryland are little more than half of what they were during the same period in the 2025-2026 season. While the 2025-2026 season saw a total of 62 RSV-related hospitalizations, the 2026-2027 cases amount to 38. Available MDH data also shows Baltimore (21%), Montgomery (29%), and Prince George's (12%) counties accounted for the most RSV hospitalizations since Oct. 4. Vaccines Help, But Hurry Vaccines help, too, but it takes about two weeks for full protection to begin. So if you’re planning on getting a vaccination, now is the time to do it. Getting vaccinated later can still help protect against illness during the rest of the season. This season’s flu shot targets H1N1, the influenza A subtype causing most reported flu infections so far, along with H3N2 and an influenza B strain. Early laboratory testing suggests the vaccine is a good match for most H1N1 viruses tested, according to the CDC, although it’s too early to know how much protection that will translate into during this flu season. This season’s updated COVID-19 vaccines target XFG, a descendant of the Omicron variant, according to the CDC. The formula was selected to better match circulating viruses, but the shots don’t guarantee protection against infection. Their main benefit remains reducing the risk of serious illness, hospitalization and death. RSV vaccines help prevent serious illness from respiratory syncytial virus, which usually causes cold-like symptoms but can lead to pneumonia and hospitalization. The CDC recommends vaccination for adults 75 and older and those ages 50 to 74 at increased risk. Unlike flu shots, RSV vaccination isn’t currently annual: People who have already received a dose shouldn’t get another at this time. Check which flu, COVID-19 and RSV immunizations are recommended for your age and health. A pharmacist or other health care provider can help sort that out, and getting vaccinated often doesn’t require a separate doctor’s visit. Pharmacies, including CVS and Walgreens, offer the shots to eligible patients, generally at no cost with most insurance. Don’t Show Up Sick Nobody wants to miss Thanksgiving dinner, but showing up sick can send more than leftovers home with the family. The CDC recommends staying home and away from others until symptoms have been improving overall and you’ve been fever-free without fever-reducing medicine for at least 24 hours. For the next five days, take extra precautions because you may still be contagious. Hosts can help by bringing in fresh air. Open windows when practical, run a portable HEPA air cleaner or take some of the gathering outside if the weather cooperates. Testing before getting together can add protection, especially when visiting someone at higher risk. But a negative rapid test isn’t an all-clear if you’re coughing, feverish or otherwise feeling sick. A well-fitting N95 or KN95 mask can also reduce risk in crowded indoor spaces, during travel or around vulnerable relatives. The familiar advice still applies. Wash your hands, cover coughs and sneezes, and clean frequently touched surfaces. Get more local news delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for free Patch newsletters and alerts

news.content_zh: Patch 于 2026 年 11 月 13 日发表的这篇文章讨论了感恩节前马里兰州呼吸道病毒的现状。报告指出,与 RSV 相关的住院人数低于上一季,但仍然存在,其中巴尔的摩、蒙哥马利和乔治王子城县的住院率最高。这篇文章强调了 疫苗接种 的重要性,特别是对于 75 岁及以上的成年人,并强调了采取预防措施的必要性,例如出现症状时戴口罩和呆在家里。虽然呼吸系统疾病的总体水平仍然较低,但文章警告说,家庭聚会期间可能会出现 传播 的情况。它还提到,疾病预防控制中心建议呆在家里直到症状改善,并在拥挤的室内空间使用口罩。该信息基于现有数据和建议,但 疫苗 的有效性存在一些不确定性。该文章作为公共卫生措施的一般指南,而不是经过确认的 暴发 报告。

Juan Pablo Torres Torretti, a pediatrics professor at the University of Chile, notes the unusual situation of empty beds in pediatric wards and intensive care units, highlighting the severity of the impact. Chile reportedly took nine months to implement protective measures for infants, though the specific nature and effectiveness of these measures are not detailed in the evidence. The article does not provide exact case or death counts, but it underscores the challenges faced by the healthcare system due to the outbreak. The focus is on the delayed response and its implications for public health, without further specifics on the scale of the outbreak or the outcomes of the measures taken.

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 18, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Reflexive Respiratory Panels Could Reduce Full-Panel Testing by 27 Percent by November 17, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Reflexive Respiratory Panels Could Reduce Full-Panel Testing by 27 Percent Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A retrospective evaluation conducted within a multi-hospital healthcare system demonstrates that implementing a customizable syndromic molecular panel with automatic reflex testing can maintain high diagnostic yields while reducing full-panel utilization by 27 percent. In an analysis of 300 sequential inpatient specimens collected across distinct seasonal periods of influenza-like illness, researchers at the Marshfield Clinic Research Institute and Marshfield Clinic evaluated the LIAISON PLEX Respiratory Flex Assay against the institutional standard-of-care BioFire Respiratory Panel 2.1. By tailoring reporting to a baseline configuration of seven high-impact pathogens and automatically reflexing negative samples to full-panel interrogation without requiring retesting, the clinical microbiology team demonstrated that diagnostic stewardship can curb unnecessary testing costs without compromising pathogen detection in symptomatic individuals presenting with acute upper respiratory tract infections. Upper respiratory tract infections remain the most prevalent global etiology of acute illness, imposing substantial clinical morbidity, mortality, and economic hardship across both adult and pediatric patient populations. In the United States alone, the annual financial impact linked to these common conditions exceeds twelve billion dollars, compounded during seasonal surges by respiratory viruses that frequently present with clinically indistinguishable signs and symptoms. During the 2024 to 2025 respiratory illness season, influenza alone generated between 610,000 and 1.2 million hospitalizations alongside an estimated 27,000 to 130,000 deaths nationwide. Because clinicians cannot reliably differentiate causative organisms based solely on bedside clinical presentation, definitive molecular testing using nucleic acid amplification tests or rapid antigen assays is essential to guide appropriate antiviral therapy, prevent unnecessary antimicrobial administration, and inform infection prevention and control practices. To navigate the expanding menu of molecular diagnostics, healthcare laboratories must constantly weigh clinical necessity, operational feasibility, and financial sustainability. Standard clinical laboratory practice frequently relies on maintaining separate platforms to accommodate varying levels of patient acuity and care settings. Low-risk outpatients seen in ambulatory clinics or urgent care settings are typically evaluated using four-target polymerase chain reaction panels restricted to SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A, Influenza B, and respiratory syncytial virus. Conversely, patients admitted to the intensive care unit with respiratory failure and multiple comorbidities may be tested on a syndromic panel covering the majority of possible respiratory infections. Verifying, maintaining, and quality-controlling multiple distinct platforms introduces substantial operational complexity, requiring duplicate validation protocols, divergent quality control schedules, and ongoing technologist competency assessments that place sustained demands on clinical microbiology resources. Discover more Research assistant services Postdoc opportunities Research report templates Learn Engineering Track Biotech The study cohort comprised 300 sequential patient specimens meeting institutional criteria for extended respiratory testing, such as intensive care unit admission, severe respiratory distress, or systemic immunocompromise, within the Marshfield Clinic Health System in northern and central Wisconsin. Testing was split evenly across two distinct seasonal epidemiologic windows designated by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention surveillance metrics: a period of low influenza-like illness spanning April through June 2024 (n = 150) and a period of elevated influenza-like illness spanning January through March 2025 (n = 150). The mean patient age in the elevated cohort was 52.2 years, significantly younger than the 62.5-year mean documented during the low-activity cohort (p = 0.002), while patient sex distributions and underlying comorbid conditions—including active malignancy, diabetes mellitus, corticosteroid therapy, and solid organ transplantation—demonstrated no statistically significant differences between the two study periods. Specimens underwent standard testing on the BioFire Respiratory Panel 2.1 followed by evaluation on the LIAISON PLEX Respiratory Flex Assay within 72 hours of collection while stored at 4 degrees Celsius. When initial evaluations revealed discrepant results between the two multiplex platforms, samples underwent additional testing performed by Diasorin using a validated two-step adjudication protocol. Nucleic acids underwent multiplex fragment analysis targeting between one and four analytes using fluorophore-labeled primers resolved by capillary electrophoresis on an Applied Biosystems 3730xl Genetic Analyzer. Amplicons meeting size and fluorescence thresholds advanced to confirmatory bidirectional sequencing, where sequences achieving PHRED quality scores of at least 20 across 90 percent of bases and minimum 100 contiguous base lengths were compared against reference sequences in the National Center for Biotechnology Information database using BLAST. Discover more Tour Colleges Cancer research funding Donate to Research Initial concordance testing between the platforms yielded an unadjusted positive agreement of 84.8 percent and a negative agreement of 97.9 percent before discordant analysis. Five clinical specimens presented with a shared single positive target alongside a discordant secondary target and were excluded from comparative calculations because they met simultaneous criteria for concordance and discordance. Of sixteen specimens positive solely by the BioFire platform, confirmatory bidirectional sequencing verified the initial finding in only two instances, one specimen was omitted due to technical processing error, and twelve returned negative results. All four specimens initially identified as positive solely by the LIAISON platform tested negative upon referee sequencing. Following the removal of unconfirmed discordant samples, post-arbitration agreement resolved to 96.7 percent positive agreement across 92 validated positive samples and 100 percent negative agreement across 186 negative specimens. Epidemiological surveillance across the two study intervals revealed pronounced seasonal variations in circulating respiratory pathogens identified by the flexible multiplex assay. During the low influenza-like illness interval, positive findings were dominated by Rhinovirus or Enterovirus at 14.7 percent (22 detections), followed by Human Metapneumovirus at 6.7 percent (10 detections), Parainfluenza Subtype 3 at 4.7 percent (7 detections), and isolated occurrences of RSV A/B and Parainfluenza Subtype 4 at 0.7 percent each, leaving 109 samples entirely negative. Conversely, testing throughout the elevated winter illness period revealed Influenza A as the most frequent pathogen at 11.3 percent (17 detections), accompanied by Seasonal Coronavirus at 6.7 percent, Enterovirus or Rhinovirus at 4.7 percent, Human Metapneumovirus and Mycoplasma pneumoniae at 4.0 percent each, RSV A/B at 3.3 percent, Adenovirus at 2.0 percent, SARS-CoV-2 at 1.3 percent, and Parainfluenza Subtype 4 at 0.7 percent. Using empirical positivity observations, clinical actionability, and severity risk, the investigators retrospectively modeled a standardized seven-target base panel configured to maximize diagnostic yield while remaining within favorable procedural reimbursement coding thresholds. The proposed core inpatient panel encompassed SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A, Influenza B, and RSV—due to their established antiviral therapeutic indications and clinical propensity to cause life-threatening complications—supplemented by seasonal Coronavirus, Enterovirus/Rhinovirus, and Human Metapneumovirus as the most prevalent circulating pathogens. Retrospective modeling demonstrated that this baseline seven-target assembly would have successfully identified 33 of 41 positive specimens during low seasonal activity, achieving an 80.4 percent diagnostic yield, and 47 of 57 positive specimens during high seasonal activity, achieving an 82.5 percent diagnostic yield relative to standard full-panel testing. A critical advantage of the customizable molecular architecture lies in software-directed reflexive reporting, which analyzes and releases masked diagnostic targets from the initial run without requiring instrument reloading, new reagent extraction, or technologist intervention. In the inpatient study cohort, coupling the seven-target base configuration to an automatic reflex protocol for negative specimens would have resolved 80 specimens on the initial tier alone, eliminating the necessity of unmasking complete panels in those patients and driving a 27 percent overall reduction in full syndromic panel utilization across the 300 evaluated cases. The authors noted that while a baseline reflex strategy could theoretically fail to capture dual infections where one pathogen resides on the base panel and a secondary coinfection resides on the masked panel, such diagnostic risks can be managed by reserving upfront comprehensive panels for critically ill ICU patients. The study also examined the diagnostic consequences of extending the seven-target design to ambulatory settings, where clinical care currently relies on standard four-target assays. Comparing diagnostic yield against standard-of-care four-target outpatient testing demonstrated an increased chance of a diagnosis during both study periods. During the low-activity period, the seven-target configuration captured 80.5 percent of potential diagnoses compared to just 2.0 percent identified by four-target testing alone, driven largely by the high prevalence of non-targeted rhinoviruses and metapneumoviruses. During elevated winter activity, the seven-target panel yielded an 82.5 percent detection rate compared to 42.1 percent for the four-target assay. The authors emphasized that providing clinicians with a definitive viral diagnosis can actively support antibiotic stewardship initiatives by discouraging unnecessary antibacterial prescribing, provided integrated clinical decision pathways link laboratory results directly to clinical management teams. Implementing flexible testing platforms also directly addresses recurring operational inefficiencies caused by duplicative testing orders within health systems. In this study, 45 percent of patients were tested with a four-target assay within 72 hours of being tested with a BioFire RP2.1 panel. Furthermore, custom and reflexive panels would have increased the laboratory's ability to respond to two scenarios that occurred during the study period: a Bordetella pertussis outbreak and a CDC request to increase influenza subtyping. Despite these demonstrable laboratory benefits, the investigators underscored critical operational and epidemiologic considerations surrounding broad-scale adoption. Limiting diagnostic reporting to customized subsets could impair the automated transmission of pathogen surveillance data to public health registries, highlighting the need for software systems that aggregate de-identified diagnostic data in the background regardless of clinical billing tiers. Furthermore, because diagnostic performance in this investigation was derived from retrospective analysis of inpatient specimens, prospective clinical validation across diverse inpatient and outpatient cohorts remains necessary to measure direct impacts on patient outcomes, turnaround times, and total cost of care under dynamic procedural reimbursement schedules. Subject of Research: Evaluation of customizable and reflexive syndromic molecular panels for respiratory pathogen detection and diagnostic stewardship Article Title: Analysis of diagnostic yield and duplicative testing reduction using a customizable and reflexive syndromic panel Article References: Pike, C., Higdon, E., Davy, K., Bulgrin, B., Arbefeville, S., & Wahlig, T. A. (2026). Analysis of diagnostic yield and duplicative testing reduction using a customizable and reflexive syndromic panel. Furthermore, custom and reflexive panels would have increased the laboratory's ability to respond to two scenarios that occurred during the study period: a Bordetella pertussis outbreak and a CDC request to increase influenza subtyping. Despite these demonstrable laboratory benefits, the investigators underscored critical operational and epidemiologic considerations surrounding broad-scale adoption. Limiting diagnostic reporting to customized subsets could impair the automated transmission of pathogen surveillance data to public health registries, highlighting the need for software systems that aggregate de-identified diagnostic data in the background regardless of clinical billing tiers. Furthermore, because diagnostic performance in this investigation was derived from retrospective analysis of inpatient specimens, prospective clinical validation across diverse inpatient and outpatient cohorts remains necessary to measure direct impacts on patient outcomes, turnaround times, and total cost of care under dynamic procedural reimbursement schedules. analysis.brief_en: This news report discusses a study conducted by researchers at the Marshfield Clinic Research Institute and Marshfield Clinic, which evaluated the effectiveness of reflexive respiratory panels in reducing full-panel testing. The study analyzed 300 patient specimens from the Marshfield Clinic Health System in Wisconsin, collected during two distinct seasonal periods: April through June 2024 (low influenza-like illness) and January through March 2025 (elevated influenza-like illness). The findings indicate that implementing a customizable syndromic molecular panel with automatic reflex testing can reduce full-panel utilization by 27 percent while maintaining high diagnostic yields. This approach allows for tailored reporting to a baseline configuration of seven high-impact pathogens, including respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and automatically reflexes negative samples to full-panel interrogation without requiring retesting. The study highlights the importance of molecular testing in guiding appropriate antiviral therapy and preventing unnecessary antimicrobial administration. The annual financial impact of upper respiratory tract infections in the U.S. exceeds twelve billion dollars, and the research underscores the need for healthcare laboratories to balance clinical necessity, operational feasibility, and financial sustainability when selecting diagnostic platforms. The results were verified through confirmatory bidirectional sequencing and compared against reference sequences in the National Center for Biotechnology Information database using BLAST.

In lung transplant recipients who are hospitalized with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection, poor outcomes are common and predicted by older age and other factors, according to study findings published in Open Forum Infectious Diseases. Recipients of solid organ transplants are vulnerable to infection in general, and those receiving new lungs are particularly susceptible to respiratory viral infections such as RSV. There is, however, limited information on risk factors for severe RSV infection outcomes in this population. To bridge this knowledge gap, researchers conducted a retrospective cohort study across 5 transplant centers in the United States and 1 each in Canada and Australia. The analysis included 155 adults (median age at RSV diagnosis, 61 [IQR, 51-67.5] years; 60% men) who underwent lung transplantation and were hospitalized with polymerase chain reaction-confirmed RSV infection between 2016 and 2019. Hospitalization for RSV occurred a median of 14 months after transplantation. More than two-thirds (68.4%) of patients received oral ribavirin, while 21.3% received inhaled ribavirin. The association between older age and severe outcomes suggests the importance of preventive strategies in this high-risk population. There was an overall decline in lung function from before to after RSV infection in a subset of patients with paired measurements — median forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) decreased from 2.01 to 1.69 L (P <.001). FEV1 declined by more than 10% in 49.2% of these patients. Regarding severe outcomes related to RSV, 58.7% of patients developed hypoxic respiratory failure, 33.5% acquired secondary fungal or bacterial respiratory infection, 17.4% required invasive mechanical ventilation during the hospital stay, and 12.3% had suspected or biopsy-proven rejection. The rate of all-cause mortality at 90 days was 7.7%, with deaths occurring a median of 21 (IQR, 16-36) days after RSV diagnosis. Logistic regression was used to explore predictors of outcomes in this population. Patients who had used oxygen prior to RSV diagnosis and those with lower respiratory tract symptoms were significantly more likely to develop hypoxic respiratory failure (odds ratios [ORs], 4.81 and 3.74, respectively). Older individuals had greater odds of requiring invasive mechanical ventilation (OR, 1.06; 95% CI, 1.02-1.12; P =.011), whereas use of oral ribavirin was associated with a lower likelihood of mechanical ventilation (OR, 0.34; 95% CI, 0.14-0.82; P =.016). In univariate analyses, use of mechanical ventilation was associated with greater odds of developing a secondary infection (OR, 3.71; 95% CI, 1.59-8.99; P =.003). Having a history of rejection in the 6 months prior to RSV infection was associated with an increased likelihood of rejection within 90 days of contracting RSV (OR, 3.23; 95% CI, 1.02-9.41; P =.035). Univariable Cox proportional hazards models revealed risk factors for 90-day mortality, including mechanical ventilation during hospitalization (hazard ratio [HR], 7.79; 95% CI, 2.47-24.60; P <.001) and time between transplantation and RSV infection (HR, 1.02; 95% CI, 1.00-1.04; P =.015). Use of oral ribavirin did not significantly influence mortality risk (HR, 5.27; 95% CI, 0.68-40.83; P =.112). Study limitations include the retrospective design, possible bias or confounding related to differences between transplant centers, the potential for residual confounding, the lack of data on RSV subtypes and ribavirin management, the absence of a non-RSV comparator group, and uncertain generalizability of the findings to nonhospitalized patients. According to the researchers, “The association between older age and severe outcomes suggests the importance of preventive strategies in this high-risk population.” References: Mendoza MA, Dumais M, Chiu CY, et al. Risk factors for hypoxia, mechanical ventilation, and mortality in lung transplant recipients hospitalized with respiratory syncytial virus: a multicenter international cohort study. Open Forum Infect Dis. Published online October 8, 2026. doi:10.1093/ofid/ofag623

In lung transplant recipients who are hospitalized with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection, poor outcomes are common and predicted by older age and other factors, according to study findings published in Open Forum Infectious Diseases. Recipients of solid organ transplants are vulnerable to infection in general, and those receiving new lungs are particularly susceptible to respiratory viral infections such as RSV. There is, however, limited information on risk factors for severe RSV infection outcomes in this population. To bridge this knowledge gap, researchers conducted a retrospective cohort study across 5 transplant centers in the United States and 1 each in Canada and Australia. The analysis included 155 adults (median age at RSV diagnosis, 61 [IQR, 51-67.5] years; 60% men) who underwent lung transplantation and were hospitalized with polymerase chain reaction-confirmed RSV infection between 2016 and 2019. Hospitalization for RSV occurred a median of 14 months after transplantation. More than two-thirds (68.4%) of patients received oral ribavirin, while 21.3% received inhaled ribavirin. The association between older age and severe outcomes suggests the importance of preventive strategies in this high-risk population. There was an overall decline in lung function from before to after RSV infection in a subset of patients with paired measurements — median forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) decreased from 2.01 to 1.69 L (P <.001). FEV1 declined by more than 10% in 49.2% of these patients. Regarding severe outcomes related to RSV, 58.7% of patients developed hypoxic respiratory failure, 33.5% acquired secondary fungal or bacterial respiratory infection, 17.4% required invasive mechanical ventilation during the hospital stay, and 12.3% had suspected or biopsy-proven rejection. The rate of all-cause mortality at 90 days was 7.7%, with deaths occurring a median of 21 (IQR, 16-36) days after RSV diagnosis. Logistic regression was used to explore predictors of outcomes in this population. Patients who had used oxygen prior to RSV diagnosis and those with lower respiratory tract symptoms were significantly more likely to develop hypoxic respiratory failure (odds ratios [ORs], 4.81 and 3.74, respectively). Older individuals had greater odds of requiring invasive mechanical ventilation (OR, 1.06; 95% CI, 1.02-1.12; P =.011), whereas use of oral ribavirin was associated with a lower likelihood of mechanical ventilation (OR, 0.34; 95% CI, 0.14-0.82; P =.016). In univariate analyses, use of mechanical ventilation was associated with greater odds of developing a secondary infection (OR, 3.71; 95% CI, 1.59-8.99; P =.003). Having a history of rejection in the 6 months prior to RSV infection was associated with an increased likelihood of rejection within 90 days of contracting RSV (OR, 3.23; 95% CI, 1.02-9.41; P =.035). Univariable Cox proportional hazards models revealed risk factors for 90-day mortality, including mechanical ventilation during hospitalization (hazard ratio [HR], 7.79; 95% CI, 2.47-24.60; P <.001) and time between transplantation and RSV infection (HR, 1.02; 95% CI, 1.00-1.04; P =.015). Use of oral ribavirin did not significantly influence mortality risk (HR, 5.27; 95% CI, 0.68-40.83; P =.112). Study limitations include the retrospective design, possible bias or confounding related to differences between transplant centers, the potential for residual confounding, the lack of data on RSV subtypes and ribavirin management, the absence of a non-RSV comparator group, and uncertain generalizability of the findings to nonhospitalized patients. According to the researchers, “The association between older age and severe outcomes suggests the importance of preventive strategies in this high-risk population.” References: Mendoza MA, Dumais M, Chiu CY, et al. Risk factors for hypoxia, mechanical ventilation, and mortality in lung transplant recipients hospitalized with respiratory syncytial virus: a multicenter international cohort study. Open Forum Infect Dis. Published online October 8, 2026. doi:10.1093/ofid/ofag623

analysis.brief_en: This report discusses a retrospective cohort study analyzing predictors of severe respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) outcomes in lung transplant recipients. Conducted across 5 U.S. transplant centers and 1 each in Canada and Australia, the study included 155 adults hospitalized with RSV infection between 2016 and 2019. Key findings indicate that older age and prior oxygen use are associated with severe outcomes, including hypoxic respiratory failure and the need for mechanical ventilation. The study also found that 58.7% of patients developed hypoxic respiratory failure, 33.5% had secondary infections, and 17.4% required invasive mechanical ventilation. The 90-day all-cause mortality rate was 7.7%. The research highlights the importance of preventive strategies in this high-risk population. However, the study has limitations, including its retrospective design, potential bias, and lack of a non-RSV comparator group. The results were published online on October 8, 2026, and the median time between transplantation and RSV infection was 14 months.

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 18, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Adjuvanted RSV Vaccine Two-Dose Regimen Enhances Immunity in Organ Transplant Recipients by November 13, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Adjuvanted RSV Vaccine Two-Dose Regimen Enhances Immunity in Organ Transplant Recipients Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A multinational phase 2b randomized trial has shown that an AS01E-adjuvanted respiratory syncytial virus prefusion F protein vaccine generates substantial immune responses in adult kidney and lung transplant recipients, with a two-dose schedule providing higher neutralizing antibody titers than a single dose. Respiratory syncytial virus poses a severe threat to individuals receiving chronic maintenance immunosuppression, yet clinical trial data evaluating specialized vaccination in this vulnerable population have remained scarce. Published in Nature Communications, the investigation, cataloged as clinical trial NCT05921903, evaluated the immunogenicity, reactogenicity, and safety of the adjuvanted vaccine over twelve months. Enrolling 386 adult participants across 48 medical centers, the trial randomized immunocompromised transplant recipients to receive either one injection or two doses spaced 30 to 60 days apart, while evaluating older non-immunocompromised adults who received a single dose as controls. The trial demonstrated that transplant recipients achieved higher neutralizing antibody titers against both RSV-A and RSV-B following a second dose, supporting targeted immunization regimens in solid organ transplant medicine. Common respiratory viruses represent a formidable clinical challenge for solid organ transplant recipients, among whom pharmacological suppression of immunity amplifies the risk of progressive infection, lower respiratory tract disease, and fatal complications. Clinical observations indicate that pneumonia and inpatient hospitalization affect more than one-third of immunocompromised adults contracting the virus. Among lung transplant recipients, infection is frequently followed by debilitating sequelae; systematic reviews indicate that nearly half of infected lung recipients experience measurable declines in pulmonary function. Furthermore, these patients confront heightened vulnerabilities to allograft dysfunction, acute cellular rejection, and chronic lung allograft dysfunction. Because available therapeutic interventions for adult respiratory syncytial virus disease remain largely supportive rather than curative, preventive vaccination strategies designed to elicit protective antibodies are vital for reducing severe clinical outcomes. Developing effective immunization regimens for organ transplant recipients is complicated by the tendency of immunosuppressive therapies to blunt vaccine responsiveness, as previously observed during vaccination against influenza, pneumococcal disease, and SARS-CoV-2. The phase 2b trial addressed this obstacle by evaluating the AS01E-adjuvanted RSV prefusion F protein vaccine, which contains 120 micrograms of recombinant RSVPreF3 antigen alongside GSK’s liposome-based AS01E adjuvant system containing 25 micrograms each of 3-O-desacyl-4′-monophosphoryl lipid A and QS-21. Conducted across 48 sites in Australia, Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan, the Republic of Korea, Spain, and the United States between July 2023 and May 2025, the trial enrolled stable adult kidney and lung transplant recipients. Researchers randomized 261 transplant recipients: 131 participants were assigned to receive a single dose, whereas 130 participants were assigned to receive two doses separated by 30 to 60 days. An additional control group of 125 non-immunocompromised adults aged 50 years or older received a single vaccine dose. Demographic and clinical baseline characteristics were balanced across groups, reflecting a representative cross-section of stable transplant recipients undergoing allograft maintenance therapy. The median age of participants was 63.0 years in the single-dose transplant group, 62.0 years in the two-dose transplant group, and 64.0 years in the control group. Kidney transplant recipients represented 70.2 percent of the single-dose group and 72.3 percent of the two-dose group, with the remainder having received lung transplants. The median interval between transplantation and vaccination was 67 months in the single-dose group and 60 months in the two-dose group. Regarding baseline maintenance immunosuppressive regimens, 99.6 percent of all transplant recipients received calcineurin inhibitors or mTOR inhibitors, 79.3 percent received corticosteroids, and 76.6 percent received mycophenolate compounds. Overall, 59.4 percent of transplant recipients were maintained on triple therapy combining calcineurin inhibitors, corticosteroids, and mycophenolate compounds. Additionally, all transplant recipients had underlying medical conditions, with metabolism and nutrition disorders being the most prevalent. The primary descriptive endpoint assessed the mean geometric increase in serum neutralizing titers against RSV-A and RSV-B in the two-dose transplant group approximately one month following the second dose relative to one month following the first dose. Among the 111 participants in the per-protocol humoral immunogenicity cohort with evaluable samples at both visits, administration of the second dose consistently boosted neutralizing antibody titers. For RSV-A, the mean geometric increase post-dose two relative to post-dose one was 1.34, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 1.20 to 1.48. For RSV-B, the mean geometric increase was 1.26, with a 95 percent confidence interval extending from 1.14 to 1.40. These measurements confirmed that administering a second dose 30 to 60 days after the initial injection induced numerically higher neutralizing titers in transplant recipients than a single dose. Results across the exposed population were similar, confirming the consistency of the booster effect across participant analyses. Humoral immunogenicity kinetics revealed contrasts between organ transplant recipients and healthy control subjects following initial vaccination, alongside sustained antibody persistence throughout twelve months. Pre-vaccination neutralizing titers exceeded assay quantification thresholds in all participants, with baseline geometric mean titers ranging from 807.0 to 889.0 ED60 for RSV-A and 864.2 to 1027.3 ED60 for RSV-B. Following initial vaccination, healthy controls exhibited rapid responses, reaching titers of 6881.3 ED60 for RSV-A and 9125.2 ED60 for RSV-B at Visit 3. In contrast, transplant recipients exhibited slower initial responses, recording titers of 3990.8 ED60 for RSV-A and 5002.9 ED60 for RSV-B in the single-dose group. Group comparisons at Visit 3 showed lower initial responses in transplant recipients, with adjusted geometric mean titer ratios of controls over combined transplant groups of 1.63 for RSV-A and 1.69 for RSV-B. Following dose two, however, neutralizing titers in two-dose transplant recipients rose to 5377.9 ED60 for RSV-A and 5820.8 ED60 for RSV-B, matching control ranges. Titers waned gradually but remained above baseline at month twelve across all cohorts. Subgroup analyses provided key insights into the clinical determinants of vaccine responsiveness, highlighting the distinct effect of antimetabolite medications on humoral immunity. In contrast, no antigen-specific CD8-positive T-cell response was detected. Clinical observations indicate that pneumonia and inpatient hospitalization affect more than one-third of immunocompromised adults contracting the virus. The study also noted that pneumonia and hospitalization affect over one-third of immunocompromised adults infected with RSV. One serious adverse event was reported, but it was classified as unrelated by the sponsor. The findings support the development of targeted immunization regimens for solid organ transplant recipients.

RSV is a leading cause of infant hospitalization; immunization offers significant protection. Parents should consult pediatricians for RSV or flu symptoms and consider preventive measures. SALT LAKE CITY — It's that time of year again. More sneezes, more coughs. Flu is already on the radar for Utah families, and with holiday gatherings coming up, health experts are also watching for RSV. For babies, even an illness that starts out looking like a cold can be harder to fight off. "Their immune system is very young. It's very immature, and they don't have the ability to fight off a lot of different viruses," said Carolyn Reynolds, executive director of the ambulatory clinical program at Intermountain Children's Health. Respiratory Syncytial Virus, or RSV, is the leading cause of hospitalization for infants nationwide. And while Reynolds said cases in Utah are low right now, she expects an uptick in the next few weeks. "I believe after Thanksgiving, before Christmas, RSV will raise its head, and we will start seeing it around," she said. RSV can look like a cold at first. Think runny nose, cough, or fever, making it hard to tell if it's RSV or the flu. Reynolds said a pediatrician can help figure out what's making your child sick. Advertise with us Report ad The CDC says to seek medical care if your child is having trouble breathing, isn't drinking enough fluids or has symptoms that are getting worse. Immunization can help protect babies from severe RSV. Expectant mothers can get the RSV vaccine between 32 and 36 weeks of pregnancy and pass protective antibodies to their babies. Eligible babies can also get an antibody shot after they're born. In the 2024-2025 RSV season, 16,000 Utah babies received protection, making them nine times less likely to end up in the hospital. And kids can get a flu shot starting at 6 months old. Families can also take simple precautions at holiday gatherings, like washing their hands often and asking guests to avoid kissing the baby's face. "Don't pass your baby around to lots of people that you don't know if they're sick or not," Reynolds said. "Take care of your kids. Do everything that you can to protect them so that you can have a really great holiday season." Parents can call their pediatrician's office or county health department to ask about a flu shot or RSV protection for their baby. Most insurance plans cover the RSV shot at no cost, and uninsured families can get it for free through Utah's Vaccines for Children program. × The Key Takeaways for this article were generated with the assistance of large language models and reviewed by our editorial team. The investigation, published in Virology Journal, detailed the virological, age-related, and clinical characteristics of positive episodes detected between January 2021 and December 2023. The study authors highlighted that comprehensive data on respiratory viral infections in western Saudi Arabia remained limited following the coronavirus disease 2019 mitigation period, establishing a clear need to describe hospital-based detections, patient characteristics, and clinical outcomes during this post-mitigation transition. To characterize the circulating pathogens, the researchers retrospectively reviewed clinical episodes in which at least one respiratory virus was confirmed through real-time polymerase chain reaction testing of nasopharyngeal specimens, primarily utilizing a multiplex diagnostic panel. Because testing denominators detailing total negative and overall test counts were unavailable in the clinical records, the investigation evaluated the relative composition and patterns among positive cases. The team applied rigorous statistical methodologies to evaluate the data, incorporating exact tests, odds ratios with corresponding 95 percent confidence intervals, Firth logistic regression modeling, and the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction to adjust for multiple hypothesis testing. The final analyzed cohort encompassed 149 real-time PCR-positive episodes occurring among 143 individual patients, though the dataset was constrained by intermittent surveillance gaps across the three-year evaluation window. Specifically, hospital clinical records were unavailable for December 2021, the nine-month span from January through September 2022, and January 2023. Among the episodes with recorded patient age, the median age was 9.0 months, with an interquartile range spanning from 3.0 to 29.0 months, while patient age was unknown or unrecorded for 32 of the episodes included in the series. Virological evaluations demonstrated that human respiratory syncytial virus was the leading pathogen, identified in 40.9 percent of the analyzed episodes, representing 61 total detections. Human rhinovirus or enterovirus was the second most prevalent viral group, documented in 34.2 percent of the episodes, making these two categories the predominant drivers of positive tests. In addition, viral co-detections involving more than one respiratory pathogen were identified in 16.8 percent of the episodes. The observed proportions of both respiratory syncytial virus and rhinovirus or enterovirus differed substantially across study years, with notable variations occurring even between identical calendar months, such as October and November, while testing sites across the medical facility also shifted over time. Age-specific analyses demonstrated that human respiratory syncytial virus detections were heavily concentrated in the youngest pediatric age brackets. Among episodes with documented patient age, 70.2 percent of all positive episodes in infants younger than 6 months were positive for human respiratory syncytial virus. This striking age concentration maintained statistical significance following Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment, yielding a corrected q-value of 0.005. Furthermore, at least 33 of the 61 total respiratory syncytial virus episodes identified throughout the entire multi-year hospital series occurred within this cohort of infants under 6 months of age. The investigators also conducted detailed evaluations linking viral identity with documented clinical presentations, but observed that symptom profiles did not reliably differentiate specific pathogens. Although a range of clinical features was documented in patient medical records at the time of presentation, no statistical association between documented symptoms and specific virus detections remained statistically significant after multiple-testing correction was applied. Pre-existing medical conditions were documented in 46.3 percent of the positive episodes across the hospital cohort and showed an initial nominal divergence based on viral classification. Specifically, underlying conditions appeared less frequent among patients with human respiratory syncytial virus, yielding an unadjusted odds ratio of 0.31 with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.14 to 0.64; however, this association did not reach statistical significance after adjustment, concluding with a corrected q-value of 0.057. Markers of acute clinical severity were substantial across the patient series: clinical specimens were collected while patients were admitted to an intensive care unit in 22.4 percent of episodes, and 9 of the 143 patients, representing 6.3 percent, had a recorded death at the time of data extraction. Addressing the broader public health context, the authors underscored that the absence of clinical testing denominators precludes interpreting these findings as measures of overall disease incidence or community seasonality, as the figures characterize only the proportional composition of positive detections. Nonetheless, the authors concluded that this single-center dataset provides vital local hospital reference data from the period immediately preceding infant respiratory syncytial virus immunization. They noted that accurately evaluating the future clinical and epidemiological impact of newly introduced infant immunization programs will require robust, denominator-based surveillance systems. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 18, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Belgian Wastewater Surveillance Correlates Strongly With Confirmed Respiratory Virus Cases by November 17, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Belgian Wastewater Surveillance Correlates Strongly With Confirmed Respiratory Virus Cases Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A nationwide validation study in Belgium demonstrated high levels of correlation between wastewater-based surveillance data and viral cases confirmed by sentinel laboratories throughout the 2024/2025 winter season. The investigation evaluated an innovative environmental monitoring framework designed to track respiratory viruses, including influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and SARS-CoV-2, across broad segments of the national population. The surveillance occurred during an exceptional respiratory virus season in which Belgium recorded the highest incidence of general practitioner visits for influenza-like illness since the COVID-19 pandemic. Substantial pressure on healthcare systems was driven primarily by concurrent epidemics of influenza and respiratory syncytial virus, while SARS-CoV-2 activity remained at comparatively low levels. Both conventional clinical reporting systems and the novel wastewater surveillance program tracked these disease dynamics simultaneously. The wastewater initiative monitored over 4.5 million inhabitants, representing approximately 38 percent of the total Belgian population, by collecting and analysing weekly samples from 30 wastewater treatment plants distributed across the country. To establish the operational validity of the environmental data, researchers compared wastewater measurements directly with figures from traditional surveillance channels. The research team computed wastewater-based epidemiological thresholds utilizing a quartile method, establishing baseline parameters to determine when viral spread reached clinically meaningful activity. Analysis confirmed that these wastewater-derived thresholds effectively monitored the circulation of influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, and SARS-CoV-2 across the target communities. The high concordance observed between wastewater metrics and laboratory-verified sentinel infections demonstrated that environmental sampling mirrored the community-level trajectory of each pathogen over the course of the season. The researchers concluded that wastewater-based monitoring provided clear added value for tracking SARS-CoV-2 compared to conventional surveillance alone, offering broad population coverage, short and consistent reporting turnaround times, and robust capabilities for pandemic preparedness. The authors also proposed several operational perspectives to refine and improve the ongoing quality of wastewater monitoring for influenza and respiratory syncytial virus. Weekly sample collection across thirty treatment plants monitored circulating respiratory pathogens throughout Belgium. Covering thirty eight percent of the population, this surveillance tracked viral presence across more than four million residents. Epidemiological thresholds determined through a quartile method allowed researchers to evaluate pathogen circulation during periods of heightened healthcare pressure. By comparing wastewater measurements directly against established surveillance systems, the study validated environmental monitoring as an effective tool for tracking community infections. High correlation between wastewater data and sentinel laboratory confirmations persisted throughout the entire winter season. The resulting findings demonstrated clear added value by providing broad population coverage alongside short and consistent reporting times. These operational strengths confirm that sewage surveillance serves as a valuable resource for pandemic preparedness during respiratory epidemics. Finally, the authors proposed several perspectives to increase the monitoring quality for both RSV and influenza in future surveillance efforts. AI生物信息学 COVID 云讲堂直播 会展中心 特价专栏 技术快讯 免费试用 生物通官微 陪你抓住生命科技 跳动的脉搏 生物通首页 > 今日动态 > 正文 已上市呼吸道合胞病毒疫苗在上市后应用场景中的成本效果:系统评价与Meta分析 《Infectious Diseases of Poverty》:Cost-effectiveness of respiratory syncytial virus vaccines in post-marketing settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年11月16日 来源:Infectious Diseases of Poverty 7.4 编辑推荐: 摘要 背景:呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)是全球范围内急性下呼吸道感染、住院及死亡的主要原因之一,在婴儿和老年人中尤为突出。本研究旨在通过合并已上市RSV疫苗的增量净效益(INB)估计值,系统总结其成本效果证据。 方法:本研究检索PubMed、Embase、Web 安捷伦 Seahorse XF Flex 分析仪开启 3D 代谢研究新时代,欢迎索取技术资料>> 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 Review Open access 摘要 背景:呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)是全球范围内急性下呼吸道感染、住院及死亡的主要原因之一,在婴儿和老年人中尤为突出。本研究旨在通过合并已上市RSV疫苗的增量净效益(INB)估计值,系统总结其成本效果证据。 方法:本研究检索PubMed、Embase、Web of Science及Cochrane Library,检索截止日期为2025年11月20日,并补充检索灰色文献与参考文献列表。分别针对老年人与婴儿开展随机效应Meta分析。研究采用人群特异性亚组分析与单因素Meta回归探讨异质性的潜在来源。 结果:系统评价共纳入17项研究,其中11项进入主Meta分析,另1项仅用于敏感性分析。在老年人中,合并INB为105.05美元[95%置信区间(CI):41.89–168.21美元;I2=93.2%]。在婴儿中,合并INB为5.81美元(95%CI:?35.44–47.07美元;I2=89.4%)。在欧洲亚组中,老年人合并INB为123.63美元(95%CI:41.23–206.02美元;I2=89.4%),婴儿为15.00美元(95%CI:?4.33–34.34美元;I2=43.4%)。留一法敏感性分析显示老年人合并INB较为稳健,而婴儿估计值对研究剔除较为敏感。 结论:在纳入研究所采用的阈值下,RSV疫苗接种在上市后应用场景中对老年人可能具有成本效果,而母体免疫接种的证据仍不确定。描述性结果提示,针对老年人的年龄与风险分层接种策略以及季节性母体免疫接种可能获得更高的INB估计值。研究间存在显著异质性,提示对合并估计值应谨慎解读,并强调在制定RSV疫苗接种政策时需考虑当地流行病学特征与实施条件。 主体内容总结 订阅安捷伦Seahorse XF出版物快报,了解实时细胞能量分析的各种应用实例领 取 背景:RSV是婴儿与老年人呼吸道疾病的重要病因。全球5岁以下儿童每年约有3300万例RSV相关急性下呼吸道感染、360万例住院及101400例死亡;高收入国家60岁及以上人群中,RSV每年约造成520万例病例、47万例住院和3.3万例院内死亡。世界卫生组织(WHO)已将RSV疫苗研发列为公共卫生优先事项。截至检索截止日,已有三款主动免疫RSV疫苗获批:Arexvy(RSVPreF3 OA,葛兰素史克,用于老年人)、Abrysvo(RSVPreF,辉瑞,用于老年人及母体免疫以保护婴儿)和mRESVIA(Moderna,用于老年人);长效单克隆抗体nirsevimab不属疫苗范畴,不在本研究范围内。既往系统评价虽总结了RSV疫苗接种的经济学证据,但未对单项经济学评价结果进行定量合并。2014年Crespo等提出以INB为共同结局指标开展成本效果研究Meta分析的框架,此后该框架已被多次应用,但尚未系统用于RSV疫苗接种的经济学证据合成。WHO免疫与疫苗相关实施研究咨询委员会(IVIR-AC)2021年指出,经济学评价的Meta分析可支持开展本国成本效果研究能力有限的国家进行决策。本研究旨在通过合并经济学评价的INB估计值,评估已上市RSV疫苗相较不接种的成本效果,并分别对老年人与婴儿进行分析。 方法:本综述未进行前瞻性注册,研究选择前已制定方案,方案及偏离情况见补充材料1;报告遵循PRISMA 2020,方法学设计与报告参考国际药物经济学与结果研究学会(ISPOR)成本与成本效果结局系统评价良好实践工作组报告。检索策略覆盖PubMed、Embase、Web of Science和Cochrane Library,检索词包括RSV、respiratory syncytial virus、vaccin、immuni、cost-effectiveness、cost-utility、economic evaluation、pharmacoeconomic*及ICER等;灰色文献检索涵盖INAHTA国际HTA数据库、Google Scholar、加拿大药物署(CDA-AMC)报告、WHO IRIS及美国CDC免疫实践咨询委员会(ACIP)会议幻灯片,并筛查纳入文献与相关综述的参考文献列表。纳入标准为:在上市后场景(评估时疫苗已上市且可从官方或公认价格来源获得本地疫苗价格)评价RSV疫苗成本效果或成本效用;比较接种与不接种;以英文发表。排除标准包括:仅关注疾病成本;评价假设价格或最大成本效果单价;缺乏独立疫苗组;无法推导INB;会议摘要或综述。文献筛选、数据提取与偏倚风险评估均由两名研究者独立完成,分歧经第三名研究者讨论解决。提取内容包括疫苗名称、价格、覆盖率、模型类型、时间跨度、研究视角、结局指标、模型人群规模、贴现率、国家收入水平、目标人群及资金来源等,并提取ICER、增量成本(ΔC)、增量效果(ΔE)与支付意愿(WTP)阈值;概率敏感性分析(PSA)散点图采用WebPlotDigitizer 4.4数字化。偏倚风险采用改良经济学评价偏倚(ECOBIAS)清单(22个条目)评估,以敏感性分析偏倚、错误模型偏倚和治疗效应相关偏倚三个关键条目进行总体分级:三项均为“是”为低风险,存在“部分/不清楚”为中等风险,存在“否”为高风险。主要结局为RSV疫苗接种相较不接种的INB,依据数据情况采用公式(1)或(2)计算,方差按公式(3)计算;K为WTP阈值,ΔE与ΔC为增量效果与增量成本,σ为标准差,ρ为ΔE与ΔC的相关系数;INB为正表示在给定阈值下具有成本效果,为负则表示不具有成本效果。数据准备分两种情形:情形1为报告ΔC、ΔE及其95%CI的研究,按近似正态假设由95%CI计算标准差;情形2为未报告离散度但提供PSA散点图的研究,数字化ΔC与ΔE的最小值与最大值,以PSA模拟次数为样本量参数,采用Wan等的方法估计标准差。ΔC与ΔE除以模型人群规模得到人均估计值;采用研究报告的WTP阈值计算INB,多阈值时选择同一国家所有纳入研究共有的阈值,未报告者由该国可比研究推算。成本按Turner等调整方法1统一换算为2023年美元:先按成本年汇率折算为美元,再用GDP隐含价格平减指数调整通胀,通胀率与汇率数据来自世界银行。统计分析采用DerSimonian-Laird法的随机效应Meta分析,分别针对婴儿与老年人进行;并分别开展单因素Meta回归。亚组分析按目标人群与地理区域、时间跨度、资金来源、疫苗类型联合分层。每项研究在每个特定人群合并分析中选取一个可估计方差的基线估计值;同一研究存在多个基线估计时,按以下层级标准取舍:医疗保健视角优先于社会视角;季节性接种优先于全年接种;目标人群与其他研究可比性最高者;评价不同疫苗时分别保留疫苗特异性估计值。异质性以I2统计量评估,仅在I2>25%时考虑;若某协变量使I2下降≥50%,则视为异质性的潜在来源。发表偏倚采用Egger检验与漏斗图评估,发现不对称时使用轮廓增强漏斗图探讨可能解释。采用留一法敏感性分析评估合并INB估计值的稳健性。分析使用Microsoft Excel 2021与R 4.3.3完成,P≤0.05为差异有统计学意义。 结果:共筛选2112条唯一记录,经题录与全文评估后17项研究纳入系统评价,其中12项进入定量合成(11项进入主Meta分析,1项仅用于敏感性分析),1项为灰色文献报告。17项研究均比较RSV疫苗接种与不接种,均在高收入国家开展且当地疫苗已上市:美国6项(35%)、加拿大2项(12%)、欧洲国家8项(47%)、中国香港1项(6%)。成人接种9项(53%),母体免疫保护婴儿8项(47%)。成人研究中,3项(18%)采用终生时间跨度,3项(18%)采用5年跨度,3项(18%)采用2年或3年跨度;婴儿研究中,7项(41%)时间跨度不超过1年,1项(6%)为5年。所有纳入研究均为模型化经济学评价:Markov模型最常见(10项,59%),其次为决策分析模型(4项,24%)、静态队列模型(2项,12%)和静态个体模型(1项,6%);无研究采用动态传播模型。Abrysvo在14项研究(82%)中被评价,Arexvy在6项(35%)中被评价,3项(18%)同时评价两种疫苗。疫苗价格范围为每剂170.38–305.70美元(2023年美元),美国最高、加拿大最低。季节性接种在部分研究中被评价。 结论:在纳入研究所采用的阈值下,RSV疫苗接种在上市后场景中对老年人可能具有成本效果,母体免疫接种的证据仍不确定。描述性结果提示,老年人按年龄与风险分层接种、母体免疫按季节接种可能获得更高INB。研究间异质性较大,合并估计值应谨慎解读,制定RSV疫苗接种政策时需考虑当地流行病学与实施条件。 打赏 展开全文 开通VIP 享海量文章 全站开放获取+解锁超过 200万篇新闻全文+每日更新 supplementary_news.content: Health & Fitness Flu, COVID-19 And RSV: What Virginians Need To Know Before Thanksgiving The CDC is tracking respiratory illnesses across the country as millions prepare to travel. Here's what they say to prepare for. Influenza is increasing in Virginia just as families prepare to gather for Thanksgiving, starting a season of togetherness that gives respiratory viruses plenty of opportunities to spread. Nationally, seasonal flu activity is increasing in many areas, while viruses that commonly cause colds are circulating at elevated levels, according to the latest update from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. COVID-19 activity is declining nationally, with emergency department visits low and decreasing. Still, wastewater monitoring shows moderate levels of the virus circulating nationwide, with some states reporting high levels. Find out what's happening in Across Virginiafor free with the latest updates from Patch. RSV, or respiratory syncytial virus, usually causes cold-like symptoms but can be serious for infants and older adults. Emergency department visits remain low nationally but are increasing in many areas. Wastewater readings for RSV and influenza A remain very low nationally. In Virginia, RSV and influenza A levels likewise are low, but growing. COVID-19 levels, at least according to some metrics, are high. Find out what's happening in Across Virginiafor free with the latest updates from Patch. In Virginia, current respiratory illness levels are low, as measured by the CDC’s acute respiratory illness metric, which tracks activity levels. In Washington, DC, Northern Virginia’s near neighbor, levels are very low. RSV levels in the state are also very low. Wastewater viral activity levels for RSV and influenza A are very low, but COVID-19 levels are high across the state, and very high in Washington, DC. Based on emergency department visits and estimates of how many people are infected by a single sick individual over time, the CDC gauges that RSV and influenza A outbreaks are growing in the state. COVID-19 is assessed as likely growing. Vaccines Help, But Hurry Vaccines help, too, but it takes about two weeks for full protection to begin. So if you’re planning on getting a vaccination, now is the time to do it. Getting vaccinated later can still help protect against illness during the rest of the season. This season’s flu shot targets H1N1, the influenza A subtype causing most reported flu infections so far, along with H3N2 and an influenza B strain. Early laboratory testing suggests the vaccine is a good match for most H1N1 viruses tested, according to the CDC, although it’s too early to know how much protection that will translate into during this flu season. This season’s updated COVID-19 vaccines target XFG, a descendant of the Omicron variant, according to the CDC. The formula was selected to better match circulating viruses, but the shots don’t guarantee protection against infection. Their main benefit remains reducing the risk of serious illness, hospitalization and death. RSV vaccines help prevent serious illness from respiratory syncytial virus, which usually causes cold-like symptoms but can lead to pneumonia and hospitalization. The CDC recommends vaccination for adults 75 and older and those ages 50 to 74 at increased risk. Unlike flu shots, RSV vaccination isn’t currently annual: People who have already received a dose shouldn’t get another at this time. Check which flu, COVID-19 and RSV immunizations are recommended for your age and health. A pharmacist or other health care provider can help sort that out, and getting vaccinated often doesn’t require a separate doctor’s visit. Pharmacies, including CVS and Walgreens, offer the shots to eligible patients, generally at no cost with most insurance. Don’t Show Up Sick Nobody wants to miss Thanksgiving dinner, but showing up sick can send more than leftovers home with the family. The CDC recommends staying home and away from others until symptoms have been improving overall and you’ve been fever-free without fever-reducing medicine for at least 24 hours. For the next five days, take extra precautions because you may still be contagious. Hosts can help by bringing in fresh air. Open windows when practical, run a portable HEPA air cleaner or take some of the gathering outside if the weather cooperates. Testing before getting together can add protection, especially when visiting someone at higher risk. But a negative rapid test isn’t an all-clear if you’re coughing, feverish or otherwise feeling sick. A well-fitting N95 or KN95 mask can also reduce risk in crowded indoor spaces, during travel or around vulnerable relatives. The familiar advice still applies. Wash your hands, cover coughs and sneezes, and clean frequently touched surfaces. Get more local news delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for free Patch newsletters and alerts
